title: Header-Based SSO (Proxy-Injected Identity)
subtitle: A reverse proxy authenticates the user and injects identity headers on its upstream request; the app trusts them because only the proxy can reach it. Step through both hops and the spoofing attempt.

steps.label: Open https://app.example.com/reports
steps.lede: The user navigates to a protected app that sits behind an access gateway. The browser will only ever talk to the proxy, never the backend directly.
steps.devtools: Open DevTools (F12) → Network, enable Preserve log. The browser only sees the browser ↔ proxy hop — the interesting identity headers live on a server-to-server hop you cannot see here.

steps.label: GET /reports (no session) → 302 to IdP
steps.lede: With no proxy session the proxy strips any inbound identity headers and redirects to the IdP. The app is never reached.
steps.devtools: On the 302 row read Location pointing at the IdP. The proxy always strips client-supplied X-Forwarded-User / REMOTE_USER before doing anything — authenticated or not. The request never reached the app.

steps.label: Authenticate at the IdP
steps.lede: The user authenticates however the proxy is configured — form, OIDC, SAML, or Kerberos. On success the IdP returns the browser to the proxy's callback.
steps.devtools: You'll see the IdP's own login pages and a callback back to the proxy. The proxy then creates its proxy session and sets a proxy session cookie.

steps.label: GET /reports (proxy session cookie)
steps.lede: After login the browser's request carries only the proxy's own session cookie — NOT any identity header. The browser must never be able to send X-Forwarded-User.
steps.devtools: In Request Headers you see only Cookie: proxy_session=…. There is deliberately no X-Forwarded-User here — the identity header is added by the proxy on its upstream hop, which the browser cannot observe.

steps.label: Proxy injects identity headers upstream
steps.lede: The proxy validates the session, resolves the user, and makes an upstream request injecting verified identity headers. This server-to-server hop is where the real credential lives.

jwt.title: Proxy-injected identity headers
payload: Authenticated username — valid ONLY because it came from the proxy, which stripped any inbound copy
Verified email from the IdP — same trust boundary
Authorization groups the app maps to permissions
Original client IP — trust only because your own edge set it (RFC 5737 doc range)

steps.devtools: This hop is not in the browser's Network tab — it is proxy→app, server-to-server. To observe it use the proxy access log, an upstream capture, or the app's request logging. The whole security model rests on the app being reachable only from the proxy (network policy, ideally mTLS on this hop).

steps.label: Spoofed header direct to app → 403
steps.lede: An attacker who forges X-Forwarded-User straight to the app's address, bypassing the proxy, is rejected — the peer is not the proxy, so the app refuses the identity header.
steps.devtools: Two defenses stop this: network policy (the app accepts connections only from the proxy, so the attacker's peer is rejected → 403) and inbound stripping (even via the proxy, a client-supplied X-Forwarded-User is overwritten before the upstream request). Watch for smuggling variants — X_Forwarded_User, duplicate headers, HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 casing.
